https://theconversation.com/who-should-h.title: Who should have a say in which species are saved? The California condor offers lessons for a global biodiversity treaty
https://theconversation.com/who-should-h.summary: When conservation affects local people, the question of who pays and who has a voice in decisions can make or break species recovery.
https://theconversation.com/who-should-h.text: In 1987, biologists captured the last free-flying condor to transfer it to captivity, and the largest flying North American bird species was officially declared extinct in the wild. Today, after decades of coordinated efforts and millions of dollars spent on captive breeding and reintroduction efforts, more than 300 condors have been restored to their natural environment. It was a victory for the species’ survival, yet this triumph was contested at nearly every step of the way. Conservationists fought bitterly over whether trapping every bird should be considered rescue or surrender. Critics argued that the cost was better spent on other threatened species. Rural communities in Utah and Arizona raised concerns about federal land-use restrictions . Hunting groups such as the National Rifle Association opposed bans on lead ammunition, a leading cause of condor deaths . The condor’s comeback illustrates several questions that governments and conservation organizations grapple with today, including which species get funded and who bears the costs. These are some of the questions being discussed at the U.N. Convention on Biological Diversity conference , being held Oct. 19-30, 2026, in Yerevan, Armenia. In 2022, countries worldwide adopted an agreement at that year’s biodiversity conference to halt and reverse biodiversity loss, known as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework . It includes goals to raise US$200 billion a year from public and private sources around the world by 2030 to conserve and manage at least 30% of the world’s land, coastal areas and oceans, stop human-caused extinctions and help struggling species survive. The agreement itself doesn’t choose which species to save, but its rules are designed to shape national conservation priorities and guide the funds that pay for conservation. Saving a species like the condor affects local communities and businesses whose activities have put those species at risk. Without local buy-in, pouring money into recovery efforts can fail, yet local communities are often left out of the discussions. An estimated 1 million species are currently threatened with extinction worldwide, and early assessments suggest the world is falling short on most of the agreement’s global biodiversity targets . Because resources are limited, conservationists must weigh trade-offs in deciding which species to protect and how. Should they fund expensive rescue efforts for a species close to extinction, or interventions likely to help multiple species at once? Or maybe they should protect organisms that are unique to a specific geographic region or a species that sustains local livelihoods. Some species are valued for what they do for humanity, such as pollinating crops or purifying water, known as ecosystem services . Honeybees, for example, pollinate over $15 billion worth of crops in the U.S. alone each year. Others hold cultural and spiritual significance, as the condor does for the Yurok Tribe in California. Many conservationists argue that living species possess an inherent right to exist independent of their usefulness to human beings. Getting support for measures to save charismatic species can be easier than for others, however. Think of Greenpeace’s “save the whales” campaign or the World Wildlife Fund’s panda logo. A panda’s adorable face can help pay for its protection and potentially the protection of its surrounding habitat , helping other species living there. A 2025 study examined more than 14,000 species-focused conservation projects from 1992 to 2016. Five mammal groups – primates, carnivores, whales, elephants and rhinos – received 86% of available funding , despite accounting for only one-third of threatened mammal projects. Plants and invertebrates, which are crucial for pollination, nutrient cycling and sustaining food webs, received only 6.6% of the financial backing. Conservation groups and economists at the Paulson Institute estimate that the world needs to spend an additional $1.3 trillion annually on biodiversity conservation and restoration to stop and reverse biodiversity loss. At the 2026 biodiversity conference, delegates will also take up another question that can make or break species recovery: When conservation affects local people, who pays and who gets a say? While conservationists celebrated efforts to return wolves to Europe over the past two decades, some farmers lost livestock to these predators and faced higher costs to protect their flocks. Current European Union funding programs help support livestock protection , but farmers’ ability to shape wolf recovery is part of the story too. Conservation can go terribly wrong if local communities aren’t consulted during planning. In the Ngorongoro Conservation Area, a protected area in Tanzania, the Maasai have fought for years against government orders that they leave the land they have lived on for generations in the name of lion conservation. In March 2026, two presidential commissions recommended that the evictions continue in order to protect wildlife, in a process that included few Maasai , Indigenous peoples’ advocates at the Oakland Institute reported. Protecting vulnerable species often means also supporting the communities living alongside them. At the last round of biodiversity talks in 2024, countries created a permanent advisory body to bring Indigenous peoples and local communities’ knowledge and decisions into the treaty’s decisions. At this year’s conference, known as COP17, they must agree on how that advisory body will operate, including whether these communities get a formal role in decision-making. They are also expected to adopt guidelines for how the 30% global conservation targets apply in Indigenous territories. The international agreement can’t dictate what happens on the ground, but its rules shape national conservation priorities and guide the funds that pay for conservation. That is why the debate over local consultation is at the heart of the 2026 talks. Conservation that is designed for people, rather than with them, risks losing the trust and local cooperation that makes recovery last. Two key issues at the conference involve guaranteeing that Indigenous peoples and local communities have a say in decisions on their territory, including how conservation programs are designed and how resources are allocated. The global biodiversity framework calls for a “ whole-of-society” approach , recognizing that protecting nature needs more than government action alone. But participation is not the same as decision-making power. Advocates for Indigenous groups say communities are too often consulted after priorities are set, rather than being involved in setting them. Whether the farmer paying for fencing or the Indigenous community with connections to a species helps set priorities or is only asked for input after the project has been approved shows whether consultation is genuine or not. The condor’s return shows that nearly extinct species can recover with help. But sustaining a species’ recovery requires protecting the conditions – and supporting the people – that make their survival possible. Researcher Garrett Ordonez, an environmental studies and international relations student at USC, contributed to this article.

https://theconversation.com/nasas-mars-o.title: NASA’s Mars orbiter fleet is getting old – here’s how that could affect future exploration
https://theconversation.com/nasas-mars-o.summary: NASA lost contact with its Maven spacecraft – the youngest of its Mars orbiters – at the end of 2025. The others in its fleet are over two decades old.
https://theconversation.com/nasas-mars-o.text: Currently, about 16,000 satellites are orbiting Earth , providing everything from GPS service and weather reports to phone service in remote locations to people across the globe. In contrast, the highest-ever number of active satellites in orbit around Mars , one of the best-explored other planets in our solar system, is eight. Starting in 2021, there were three from NASA, two from the European Space Agency and one each from the Indian Space Research Organization, the UAE Space Agency and the China National Space Administration. The oldest of these is still 2001 Mars Odyssey, which has now spent 25 years in space, with Mars Express, at 23 years, and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, at 20 years, hot on its heels. But in December 2025, NASA lost contact with its Maven spacecraft , bringing the total number of active satellites down to seven, and NASA’s to two. The cause of the loss of Maven has still not been publicly released, and NASA officially declared the mission over in June 2026. A final report on the cause of the loss is due later this year. NASA is exploring potential commercial solutions to supplement the current fleet of Mars orbiters. In September 2026, NASA selected Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin to provide a Mars telecommunication satellite no later than Dec. 31, 2028. These satellites are important because future missions will rely on them to communicate with Earth and select safe landing sites on Mars. Planetary scientists like me rely on the data they’ve taken over the past few decades to learn more about our close, red neighbor. The Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN, or Maven, spacecraft arrived at Mars in 2014, making it NASA’s youngest orbiter. It was only briefly the youngest in the international Mars family, as the Indian space agency’s Mars Orbiting Mission spacecraft arrived a few days later. The longer any satellite spends in space, the greater the toll of the harsh environment – from extreme temperature swings to solar radiation . Maven, however, appeared generally healthy until it missed a radio check-in – a sign of trouble – after emerging back from behind the planet. Whatever happened to Maven last December was only the second time in the 21st century that NASA had lost contact with an orbiter during otherwise ordinary operations. The other time was in 2006, with Mars Global Surveyor , which NASA ultimately lost, likely due to issues with uploaded software commands. The Mars exploration community, myself among them, is waiting with bated breath to understand why one-third of NASA’s Mars fleet lost contact seemingly overnight. The loss ends a stellar, almost two-decade-long track record of missions ending when expected, not before. Mars science has been in a golden age since 2001 Mars Odyssey arrived at the red planet 25 years ago. NASA has had a Mars rover of some type operating on the surface continuously since 2004 with the Exploration rover landings , so there have been only a handful of years in the 21st century where scientists couldn’t access nearly simultaneous views of Mars from the surface and from orbit. This access gives Mars scientists the ability to study how both the surface and atmosphere change over time. In particular, we can follow changes with Mars’ seasons , which drive about a quarter of its atmosphere onto its surface as seasonal ice . And we have found laundry lists of these changing features, including “spiderlike” araneiform features in the soil that likely develop from carbon dioxide geysers. Learning about rare events like global dust storms , which obscure Mars’ entire surface, also opens up many new questions. We still don’t know what triggers the start of a global dust storm, and they only occur every several Mars years. In Maven’s 11 years at Mars, it was only able to observe one global dust storm, in 2018 . From a practical standpoint, Mars orbiters have their own science missions. However, their powerful radios are also critical for delivering data from landers and rovers , like Perseverance or Curiosity, back to Earth. In the past, NASA has adjusted the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and Maven orbits to support landings and surface operations. HiRISE (High-Resolution Imaging Science Experiment) aboard the Reconnaissance orbiter, is the highest-resolution camera in orbit to date. Engineers have used data from HiRISE to ensure they could deliver the Mars rovers Curiosity and Perseverance to the surface, as well as the InSight lander . While Mars orbiters and their instrument suites are selected for their science value, they have come to participate in infrastructure that is essential for getting all the possible data back to Earth. These tasks, which go beyond science data collection, make the orbiter fleet critical to Mars exploration. The Dec. 31, 2028, delivery date for the Blue Origin telecommunications Mars orbiter to NASA represents the earliest a new orbiter could be launched for Mars. Mars launch opportunities happen at an approximately 2-year cadence, when Mars and Earth get closest to each other in their respective orbits. During this window, less fuel is needed for the journey. If a new Mars orbiter for science or telecommunications is not launched by the 2028 window, the next opportunity would be in 2030 or 2031. While the Blue Origin telecommunications orbiter would support future exploration missions, the announcement did not outline plans for any science instrumentation onboard. Mars Odyssey will be around 30 years old by then, and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter around 25. NASA hardware tends to be hardy, often greatly exceeding expectations. For example, the Mars Exploration rovers were meant to last for 90 days, with Spirit ending its mission after over six years and Opportunity after over 14 years. However, orbiters may slowly lose capability over time – the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter’s spectrometer instrument ceased operations in 2023 , while its other instruments are still active. But three or four decades in a space environment is a long tour of duty for any hardware in space, let alone hardware that is pulling double-duty as scientist and radio broadcaster. Much like driving your first car for far longer than you had planned on, the NASA orbiter fleet is waiting to see if the next repair bill means it’s time for an upgrade, or if it’ll have to catch rides from its friends. Until NASA releases its report, scientists and engineers will be waiting to understand what happened to end the Maven spacecraft’s mission early, and how those details can help them keep the current fleet flying until reinforcements finally arrive.

https://theconversation.com/for-centurie.title: For centuries, bird migration was a mystery – a tech revolution is changing that, and could help save these amazing creatures
https://theconversation.com/for-centurie.summary: An early clue came from storks found in Europe with African arrows in their bodies. Today, an atlas reveals hundreds of bird migration routes that are both complicated and remarkable.
https://theconversation.com/for-centurie.text: For more than 2,000 years , scientists have scratched their heads over one of the most basic mysteries of the natural world: Where do birds go? Billions of birds appear and disappear with the seasons every year. Early naturalists offered explanations for the disappearances that today seem fantastical: Birds transformed into other species , one theory went. Others suggested they hibernated underwater or even migrated to the moon . The truth, that these small animals were traveling thousands of miles across the planet, must once have seemed just as improbable. Then, in the early 1800s, dramatic evidence emerged supporting the theory of migration. White storks began appearing in Germany with African arrows embedded in their bodies. These birds became known as pfeilstörche , or “arrow storks .” They provided compelling evidence that birds disappearing from Europe were traveling all the way to Africa and back. Almost two centuries later, scientists are still asking the same question, but our ability to answer it has been transformed. For most of ornithological history, scientists understood migration through brief glimpses of a bird, a specimen collected somewhere else, or the rare instance of a banded bird recovered hundreds or thousands of miles from where it had been marked. From these fragments of intelligence, scientists reconstructed journeys that took place largely beyond their view. Today, it’s possible to see the journeys themselves, almost in real time. Bird banding was the first tool used to attempt a systematic approach to connect these fragments of information. Since the early 1900s, researchers have placed uniquely numbered metal bands on birds and hoped someone, somewhere, would encounter them again. Of more than 79 million birds banded, only about 6.5 million have been recovered . That generally told scientists just two things: where a bird was banded and where it was encountered again. Everything between them remained invisible. Over the past quarter-century or so, the tools used to determine where birds go have changed dramatically. Tracking devices can now be carried by increasingly smaller birds, recording their movements and communicating with land-based receivers or satellites orbiting the earth. Testing stable isotopes in feathers and other tissues can reveal where a bird originated. Genetic testing can distinguish populations. At the same time, the extraordinary growth of bird-watching and citizen science has created another revolution. Millions of observations by bird-watchers submitted to eBird , an online database to record the birds they see, show the distribution and abundance of birds across a continent throughout the year in ways early ornithologists could scarcely have imagined. Collectively, these methods open an extraordinary new window into migratory birds and one of nature’s most remarkable behaviors: migration. More than 70% of North American bird species are migratory. Yet scientists have known surprisingly little about where specific populations go. A species like the American robin may breed across thousands of miles of North America, with different breeding populations migrating to entirely different places for the winter. Birds breeding in one part of the continent may travel one route and encounter one set of environmental conditions, while members of the same species experience a completely different set of conditions along another route. These connections between where a bird breeds and where it spends the winter is called migratory connectivity . They are critical for understanding everything from the consequences of climate change on birds to how avian pathogens and diseases spread, to a species’ basic ecology. We are ornithologists and conservation scientists who have spent almost 15 years along with a team of contributors compiling this rapidly expanding knowledge on bird movement into The Atlas of North America’s Migratory Birds . It is being published Nov. 3, 2026, by Princeton University Press, with all profits going to bird conservation and research in Latin America and the Caribbean. The atlas covers the latest information on seasonal movements for nearly 600 species and combines a century of bird-banding data with eBird observations, tracking studies, stable isotope testing, genetics and other sources of information. What emerges is a picture of migratory birds that is both more complicated and more remarkable than the simple arrows pointing between breeding and wintering ranges on a map. Consider the yellow-billed cuckoo . These birds breed over a wide range of the eastern two-thirds of the U.S. but migrate to a relatively small wintering area in the Gran Chaco region of northern Argentina, Paraguay and southern Bolivia. In contrast, peregrine falcons that breed in Alaska migrate almost directly south, dispersing across the Americas to wintering grounds that extend as far as southern South America. Discoveries like these are accumulating rapidly. Collectively, they amount to a renaissance in our understanding of animal movement never before imagined. The more clearly scientists can follow individual birds and populations across the planet, the more extraordinary these species can seem. Migratory birds such as the arctic tern and northern wheatear cross oceans, deserts and mountain ranges. Some, like the bar-tailed godwits, fly thousands of miles without stopping . Others, like the American redstart, return year after year to remarkably precise breeding and wintering locations. They navigate landscapes and respond to winds, weather, food and environmental conditions across enormous geographic scales. We see these species and their migrations as among evolution’s great living masterpieces. That’s why we combined science with natural history and artist John Anderton’s extraordinary illustrations of the birds themselves. The maps allow us to see where birds travel, and the art brings the species to life. Together, they make visible something that humans could only imagine for most of our history. North America has lost about 3 billion birds during the past half-century, and many migratory species continue to decline. To understand why a population is declining and help save it, researchers need to understand the species’ entire annual cycle: its critical stopover habitats, wintering grounds and threats along its migration routes. For much of the history of ornithology, scientists studied birds primarily during their breeding season. That made practical sense. Birds are conspicuous then – singing, defending territories, building nests and raising young. But a migratory bird may spend only a few months of its life in its breeding grounds. Conditions such as weather, food availability and habitat quality encountered during migration can determine whether an individual survives to breed again . Drought thousands of miles away can affect a bird’s condition months later. American redstarts depart later after dry winters and produce fewer young . Declining horseshoe crab populations in Delaware Bay have reduced food availability for migrating red knots , contributing to lower survival . All of this knowledge has accumulated because people value birds and have devoted enormous time and effort to understanding them. For more than a century, thousands of bird-banders have woken up before the crack of dawn to set traps, carefully place bands on birds’ legs and release them, often knowing the chances of ever learning what happened to those individuals were exceedingly small. More recently, tracking technology has allowed researchers to follow individual birds across continents and oceans . Those tracks exist because scientists, students, technicians and others have spent countless hours attaching and recovering tags, and contributing and sharing their data. Today, millions of bird-watchers contribute observations that, thanks to advances in data science, allow us to watch migration unfold across an entire continen
facts: For more than 2,000 years , scientists have scratched their heads over one of the most basic mysteries of the natural world: Where do birds go?
Then, in the early 1800s, dramatic evidence emerged supporting the theory of migration.
Since the early 1900s, researchers have placed uniquely numbered metal bands on birds and hoped someone, somewhere, would encounter them again.
Of more than 79 million birds banded, only about 6.5 million have been recovered .
Over the past quarter-century or so, the tools used to determine where birds go have changed dramatically.
More than 70% of North American bird species are migratory.

We are ornithologists and conservation scientists who have spent almost 15 years along with a team of contributors compiling this rapidly expanding knowledge on bird movement into The Atlas of North America’s Migratory Birds .
It is being published Nov. 3, 2026, by Princeton University Press, with all profits going to bird conservation and research in Latin America and the Caribbean.

The atlas covers the latest information on seasonal movements for nearly 600 species and combines a century of bird-banding data with eBird observations, tracking studies, stable isotope testing, genetics and other sources of information.
North America has lost about 3 billion birds during the past half-century, and many migratory species continue to decline.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-acupunctur.title: Acupuncture and mutual exchange in Chinese and Soviet science

https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Scientists discover a hidden messaging system deep inside the brain
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A tiny region deep within the brain has surprised scientists by revealing a remarkably sophisticated communication system. Previously thought to broadcast the same chemical signal throughout the brain, this region actually sends targeted messages that help control learning, attention, and behavior, according to new research in mice.
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: Deep within the brainstem is a tiny group of nerve cells that plays an outsized role in how the brain functions. This region, called the locus coeruleus (LC), gets its name from the Latin words for "blue place." Although it contains only a small fraction of the brain's neurons, it produces norepinephrine (NE), a chemical messenger that helps regulate attention, learning, heart rate, and the body's reactions to stress and excitement. Scientists have long assumed that the LC operates like a loudspeaker, sending essentially the same norepinephrine signal across the brain. However, a new study published in Nature challenges that understanding. Using brain imaging, recordings of neural activity, genetic techniques, and behavioral experiments in mice, researchers at the Allen Institute discovered that the LC communicates through several distinct pathways. Rather than broadcasting one general message, it delivers signals to specific destinations, with different groups of neurons responding to different experiences. By tracing the connections of LC neurons, researchers found that different groups of cells communicate with specific regions of the nervous system. These pathways determine where signals trigger the release of norepinephrine, creating a much more organized communication network than previously recognized. Neurons in the upper (dorsal) portion of the LC primarily connect to the cerebral cortex and forebrain. Meanwhile, cells in the lower (ventral) portion send their signals mainly to the brainstem and spinal cord. This arrangement allows different parts of the LC to influence separate brain functions. "The findings suggest the brain's norepinephrine system is far more like a targeted postal network than a foghorn," said Karel Svoboda, director of Neural Dynamics at the Allen Institute and study co-author. Understanding how this signaling network is organized could eventually change how certain neurological and mental health conditions are treated. Norepinephrine plays a central role in regulating attention and mood, making it an important target for medications used to treat depression, anxiety, and ADHD. Neurons in the LC are also among the earliest brain cells to deteriorate in Alzheimer's disease, suggesting that the new findings could have implications for understanding and treating these conditions. Current treatments that influence norepinephrine can affect multiple brain circuits at once, sometimes producing beneficial effects in one region while causing unwanted effects elsewhere. A clearer map of the LC's specialized pathways could help scientists develop therapies that act more selectively on the circuits involved in particular symptoms. The research received support from the National Institutes of Health's Brain Research Through Advancing Innovative Neurotechnologies ® Initiative, also known as The BRAIN Initiative®. The researchers also uncovered an important distinction between the functions of different LC neurons. Cells in the dorsal LC that connect to the cortex were particularly active during learning. When mice performed decision-making tasks and adjusted their choices after an unfavorable result, these neurons increased their activity. Neurons in the ventral LC behaved differently. Their activity rose shortly before mice ignored signals indicating that a reward might be available. This suggests that these cells help regulate whether animals respond to opportunities in their surroundings. "What emerged was a clear map: neurons in the dorsal LC that send signals upward to the cortex are involved in learning, whereas neurons in the ventral region projecting downward to the brainstem and spinal cord govern whether animals engage with their environment at all," said Svoboda. "We also showed that these anatomical differences are mirrored by distinct gene expression patterns." These findings indicate that the differences between the two groups extend beyond their locations and connections. They also have distinct patterns of gene activity that reflect their specialized roles. The study involved an extensive examination of the mouse brain. Scientists used whole-brain imaging to study nearly 35,000 neurons, analyzed the genetic profiles of almost 400,000 cells, and reconstructed the complete structures of several exceptionally complex nerve cells. During this work, they encountered another remarkable finding: LC neurons possess extraordinarily long axons. These projections carry signals from nerve cells to other cells, allowing information to travel across the nervous system. The researchers found that LC axons measured approximately 35 centimeters long on average. One particularly extraordinary axon had a total reconstructed length of 70.32 centimeters, making it part of the longest single neuron ever measured in a mouse. "This neuron, like many others that we studied, supplies NE to a very large volume of the cerebral cortex. For the brain, this is highly unusual. Most neurons are more specific in their targets," said Jeremiah Cohen, scientist at the Allen Institute and study co-author. "But this neuron doesn't release NE everywhere. It ignores the cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal cord." Despite its remarkable length and extensive reach, the neuron does not distribute norepinephrine throughout the entire brain. Instead, its connections remain selective, reinforcing the discovery that the LC operates through carefully organized signaling pathways. The researchers also identified intriguing similarities between the norepinephrine system and the brain's dopamine signaling system. Dopamine is another major chemical messenger that sends signals to the basal ganglia, a brain region involved in forming habits. Scientists suspect that dopamine and norepinephrine work together to support learning, potentially allowing the brain to acquire several complex and abstract concepts at the same time. By revealing the intricate connections, specialized functions, and unusual physical structure of neurons in the locus coeruleus, the research provides a more detailed picture of how the animal brain communicates and learns. Although the findings come from experiments in mice, they could eventually help scientists better understand human brain function and design treatments that target specific neural circuits rather than affecting entire signaling systems. https://phys.org/news/2026-10-world-glac.summary: Glaciers ending in lakes, oceans or ice shelves make up 3.2% of the world's glaciers, but lost 134 billion metric tons (148 billion tons) of ice each year between 2000 and 2019, accounting for more than half of all glacier ice loss, a new study shows.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-taiwan-typ.title: Taiwan shuts down as Typhoon Champi approaches
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-taiwan-typ.summary: Most shops and schools were shut across Taiwan on Friday as Typhoon Champi neared the island, forcing hundreds of people to leave their homes ahead of the powerful storm.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-europe-kil.title: Europe's killer heat this summer claims 50,000 lives. Climate change blamed for two-thirds of deaths
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-europe-kil.summary: Blistering record heat in Europe this summer helped kill more than 50,000 people, with nearly two-thirds of that death toll blamed on human-caused climate change, a new study found.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-based-meth.title: Light-based method enables precise control of ultrafast electron flow in a scanning tunneling microscope
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-based-meth.summary: What would it take to watch an electron move through a material? Researchers would need to see individual atoms and capture an electron's motion at incredibly short timescales. A Technion-led team has brought those two capabilities together in a scanning tunneling microscope, using carefully shaped laser pulses to control the direction of electron flow while preserving nanoscale spatial resolution.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-dead-tissu.title: Costly dead-tissue disorder in apples caused by faster growth rates
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-dead-tissu.summary: New research reveals that faster growth rates in Honeycrisp apples increase both the incidence and severity of the "bitter pit" disorder, which is responsible for large-scale fruit yield losses and avoidable economic impacts for apple producers and storers.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: What can people who remember everything teach us about the brain?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: Without looking back at an appointment calendar or diary or searching Google, what can you recall about the day of Nov. 5, 2021? Unless that date happens to hold an anniversary or other special meaning, probably not too much.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.title: Diagnostic uncertainty: Why losing a diagnosis can be as difficult as receiving one
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.summary: When actor Christina Applegate revealed that she had been misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS), she described the experience as "very unnerving" and "really confusing."

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: Study finds patients experienced rapid weight gain after starting antipsychotic medication
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: People with severe mental illness experienced more rapid increases in both weight and long-term blood sugar levels during the first three months after starting treatment with antipsychotic medication, according to a study from Karolinska Institutet and University College London published in The Lancet Psychiatry.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: AI gets more diagnoses right than generalist doctors in medical challenge
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: One of the many challenging parts of being a doctor is diagnosing exactly what is wrong with a patient. This is because numerous illnesses often have overlapping symptoms, which can make the diagnostic journey a long one.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: Using AI in the global fight against HIV
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: When faced with the possibility of an HIV diagnosis, sometimes the best initial prescription is support from a trusted friend—someone who might offer not just emotional guidance but also critical, practical health resources. A Harvard research team thinks artificial intelligence has a role to play in that process.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Children who eat more ultraprocessed foods show stronger brain responses to appetizing foods
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: Children who eat more ultraprocessed foods (UPFs) show stronger responses in the brain's reward network when viewing images of appetizing foods—and these brain responses are linked to increases in body fat one year later.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: AI breast cancer survival model could improve accuracy and personalize care
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: New University of Cincinnati Cancer Center research published in the Journal of Statistical Theory and Practice describes the potential for a more robust and accurate breast cancer survival model that combines statistical methods with a deep learning framework. The goal is to give physicians a better tool to make personalized care decisions for each patient.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.title: Tackling diabetes with an electronic implant: How a tiny catalyst lowers blood sugar
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.summary: Type 2 diabetes is becoming increasingly common worldwide. Unlike type 1 diabetes, it is often linked to obesity, a sedentary lifestyle and excess energy intake over many years. Although insulin injections can bring blood sugar levels down, they do not address the body's chronic energy surplus. Insulin merely helps muscle cells take up glucose from the bloodstream, but if the body does not use that energy, the excess is converted into fat. This helps explain why many patients continue to gain weight despite treatment.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: AI tool may support dermatologists in assessing skin lesions for cancer risk
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers have found that an artificial intelligence (AI) tool may provide dermatologists with additional information to help assess whether skin lesions are cancerous and inform their clinical decisions about whether to biopsy or monitor them, according to a study published in Mayo Clinic Proceedings.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.title: The tendency to imitate others is shared across 22 countries, study finds
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.summary: People often imitate some of the actions and gestures of others they are observing, without deliberately trying to do so. This tendency, known as automatic imitation, has long been assumed to be universal.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: Who decides when medical AI may be updated?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: Medical AI can improve with new patient data, but every update must be checked first. Patients, equipment and ways of working change, and a model trained on older data can gradually get worse without anyone noticing.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.title: Gut microbiome may help explain why sleep improvement varies after hydrogen supplementation
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.summary: A Hiroshima University–led clinical trial found that hydrogen supplementation did not significantly improve sleep quality compared with a placebo; however, exploratory analyses suggest that differences in the abundance of hydrogen-producing gut bacteria may be associated with individual differences in sleep-related responses.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.title: How much autonomy do women actually have when giving birth?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-a.summary: You spend your pregnancy researching and planning for when your baby finally arrives, as well as considering what might happen if things don't go according to plan.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-w.title: 4 ways to help your body adjust to the fall time change
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-w.summary: An extra hour in bed sounds like a good deal. But while our phones may update to the fall time change automatically, our body clock isn't quite so quick. You may even find yourself waking up earlier than normal and ready for bed before your evening has properly begun.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-w.title: Women are more optimistic about aging—until memory problems emerge
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-w.summary: A study, published in the Journal of Women & Aging, found memory complaints were linked to negative expectations about aging in people with mild cognitive impairment as well as cognitively healthy adults.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.title: Plant-first food pyramid brings international dietary guidelines together in adaptable global guide
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.summary: Dietary guidance varies by country, and no international food pyramid has brought its recommendations together until now. BYU nutritional science professor Karen Della Corte led a global team of nutrition scientists to develop an International Food Guide Pyramid that reflects broad scientific agreement and can be adapted across cultures and borders.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.title: Updated cancer treatment framework offers new guidance on actionability and resistance biomarkers
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-c.summary: ESMO has published version 2 of the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (ESCAT), a major update to the internationally recognized precision oncology framework that helps oncologists assess the clinical relevance of molecular alterations and match patients with the most appropriate targeted therapies.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.title: Can Reddit help strengthen health communications on extreme heat?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.summary: Two years ago, Robbie M. Parks, an environmental health scientist at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health, and Nathaniel Matthews-Trigg, director of climate and disaster resilience at Americares, founded an online community on Reddit, r/heat_prep, where members share information and advice about coping with extreme temperatures.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: Mindfulness and self-compassion can alleviate premenstrual symptoms
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: A kind attitude toward oneself and practicing mindfulness can improve functioning in individuals who experience severe premenstrual symptoms, according to a study by psychologists from SWPS University and Jagiellonian University.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.title: Blood test can help clinicians better identify brain injury severity in patients
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-b.summary: Clinician-scientists hope to expand the use of blood-based biomarker tests for traumatic brain injury (TBI) to improve identification and escalation of care for patients whose diagnosis otherwise might be missed.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-k.title: First-of-its-kind trial tests low-dose radiation to target brain inflammation in Parkinson's disease
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-k.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers are studying whether low-dose radiation therapy can slow the progression of Parkinson's disease by targeting inflammation in areas of the brain affected by the disease. The clinical trial is the first to investigate low-dose radiation as an anti-inflammatory approach in patients with early-stage Parkinson's disease.

https://theconversation.com/why-ultra-or.title: Why ultra-Orthodox parties hold so much sway in Israeli politics
https://theconversation.com/why-ultra-or.summary: Ultra-Orthodox Jews, often called Haredim, make up a small but growing percentage of Israel’s population. Still, their political parties wield significant influence.

https://theconversation.com/fear-based-c.title: Fear-based campaign ads can grab attention, but whether they win votes is less clear
https://theconversation.com/fear-based-c.summary: Political campaigns often use fear to play on voters’ existing prejudices and stereotypes. What that means for your vote is less predictable.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-habitat-fi.title: Habitat explains Finnish animal distributions better than climate, study finds
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-habitat-fi.summary: Researchers at the University of Helsinki wanted to understand which is the dominant factor for species occurrence and abundance: the climate or habitat-related variables, such as their natural state and the share of land shaped by human activity. Solutions to mitigate biodiversity loss depend on the answer to this question.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-power-stud.title: Power cuts and sleep: Students link load shedding to anxiety, disrupted rest and lower grades
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-power-stud.summary: South Africa endured its worst year of load shedding (scheduled power cuts by the country's utility, Eskom) in 2023. The power went off on 335 of the year's 365 days, often several times a day. Since then, the country has gone more than a year and a half without these planned power cuts.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-reveal-imm.title: Glowing plants reveal immune responses around infection sites via two colors
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-reveal-imm.summary: Researchers at the MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences (LMS) have developed a new way to make glowing biological reporters more accurate, allowing scientists to track gene activity in living plants over days, weeks and potentially even months and years. The approach could help researchers study how plants respond to disease, pests and environmental stress, while opening the door to similar applications in animal and human disease models.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-human-side.title: Study maps the human side of flood risk
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-human-side.summary: When heavy rain hits a city, knowing where water will accumulate is only part of the picture. Who lives in the affected buildings? How might flooding disrupt their lives? And where could additional support make the greatest difference?

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-magnetic-f.title: Counting magnetic flux quanta offers new way to measure photon numbers
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-magnetic-f.summary: Researchers at AIST have directly observed magnetic flux quanta generated in a superconductor by photon absorption and demonstrated a new principle of photon detection that identifies the number of photons based on the number of these flux quanta.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-pretty-tox.title: 'It's pretty toxic… but just a little, I want to be like that': What young men think of manosphere content
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-pretty-tox.summary: Masculinity content promises young men self-optimization and success, but often delivers health harms, risk-taking, unattainable standards, gender stereotypes and misogyny. The latter is the strongest predictor of violent extremism.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists.title: Scientists demonstrate AI-designed enzyme for drug synthesis
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists.summary: The new RFD4-Proteina unified generative model for protein design—created by the Institute for Protein Design (IPD) in collaboration with NVIDIA—uses advanced AI to generate entirely new protein sequences and structures, achieving computational design success rates five to 10 times higher than previous models and generating candidates five to 10 times faster.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-chemically.title: Chemically modified sugars enable direct nanostructure formation
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-chemically.summary: Researchers at AIST have demonstrated the synthesis of nanoporous carbonaceous materials and carbonaceous materials with layered nanostructures through a simple process involving the chemical modification of common sugars such as sucrose and fructose.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-psychology.title: The psychology of why we overpay for used cars—study points to left-digit bias
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-psychology.summary: Consumers routinely ignore information when making purchases. They overlook the tax attached to a price, skim past ingredient lists and often fail to process exact numbers with any precision.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-adsorbents.title: Designing better adsorbents to remove PFAS from water
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-adsorbents.summary: A review by Tohoku University researchers identifies key molecular features that could guide the development of more effective materials for removing PFAS from water. The study is published in the journal ACS Materials Au.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-plain-sili.title: Plain silicon grating reveals a hidden 'twist' in light from electron beams
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-plain-sili.summary: In 1953, two physicists showed that an electron beam skimming past a grating emits light whose color depends only on the electron's speed and the grating's spacing. Known as Smith-Purcell radiation, this phenomenon has become a useful tool for building compact, tunable light sources and tracking particle beams without touching them.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-elections..title: Elections are more predictable than they look
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-elections..summary: As politics in America become more polarized and each voting cycle seems more fraught than the last, a common narrative in the media is that each election is unique and increasingly unpredictable. But new research shows that congressional elections follow strong statistical patterns, even when individual races produce surprises.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-bacteria-r.title: Bacteria reinvent their weapons through selection, chance and gene swapping
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-bacteria-r.summary: Many of the most potent antibiotics originate from bacteria. A large proportion belong to a class of compounds known as nonribosomal peptides (NRP). They are produced by large bacterial enzyme machineries—the nonribosomal peptide synthetases, or NRPS for short. These function like molecular assembly lines: Similar to the stations in a car factory, where new parts are added to the car at each step, several specialized modules string together amino acid by amino acid to build a peptide.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-marker-pan.title: New marker panel and free web tool help track stem cells as they develop
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-marker-pan.summary: How can the identity of pluripotent stem cells be determined more reliably during their differentiation? Researchers from the IUF—Leibniz Research Institute for Environmental Medicine and Heinrich Heine University Duesseldorf have systematically validated marker genes for this purpose and developed a web-based application for the automated classification of early cell fates. The study has been published in Stem Cell Reports.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-antibiotic.title: Can we stop antibiotic resistance from ruining promising drugs before they reach patients?
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-antibiotic.summary: What if we could predict early in drug development which antibiotics bacteria are most likely to become resistant to? In a review published in Nature Reviews Microbiology, researchers from the HUN-REN Biological Research Centre, Szeged (HUN-REN BRC Szeged) and the Hungarian Centre of Excellence for Molecular Medicine (HCEMM) in Szeged propose a five-step decision-making framework that could help identify resistance risks early, refine promising drug candidates and prevent costly failures.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-potatoes-s.title: Potatoes could be the secret to better plant-based meat, say food scientists
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-potatoes-s.summary: Potatoes could hold the key to making better gluten-free plant-based meat, according to a new study.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-everyday-m.title: Everyday Mylar turned into a promising insulator for lunar habitats
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-everyday-m.summary: Establishing a long-term presence on the moon will require solving challenges that are easy to overlook on Earth. Lunar temperatures, for instance, can vary from hundreds of degrees below zero to boiling, making effective insulation essential for lunar habitats.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-chaos-move.title: Chaos makes sense of market movements in a crisis
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-chaos-move.summary: Research shows that crises do more than cause financial market volatility and falling share prices—they lead to markets becoming far more interconnected.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-stellar-co.title: Stellar collision may explain why Orion Nebula's planet-forming disks appear younger than its stars
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-stellar-co.summary: The Orion Nebula is a large star-forming region visible to the naked eye. Some of the young stars in the nebula are surrounded by disks of gas and dust in which planets form. Radiation from the massive central star, 1 Ori C1 (Theta-1 Orionis C1), gradually strips material from these disks, giving them shapes that resemble tadpoles.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists.title: Scientists uncover the molecular pillars that shape our cells' powerpacks
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists.summary: Mitochondria are the tiny powerpacks that supply most of the energy our cells need. Their ability to generate this energy relies on a distinctive architecture: two membranes, one tucked inside the other, separated by a narrow gap called the intermembrane space (IMS). This tiny space helps sustain the chemistry of energy production, making its organization critical to how these cellular powerpacks function.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-mechanism-.title: Mechanism behind PARP1-mediated DNA repair characterized, offering insight into targeted cancer therapy
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-mechanism-.summary: When DNA is damaged, cellular processes respond and repair the DNA. Inhibiting DNA damage repair can be therapeutically beneficial in cancers with genetic vulnerabilities related to DNA damage response. Scientists at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital have uncovered a mechanism behind how this process works, which may have implications for cancer treatment. The results were published today in Molecular Cell.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-rare-fossi.title: Rare fossils reveal what ancient Denisovans may have looked like
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-rare-fossi.summary: Whenever anything is written about the Denisovans, the word "mysterious" is almost guaranteed to appear. That is because we just don't know a lot about this extinct human group that may have lived in East Asia from at least 300,000 to 45,000 years ago and was closely related to the Neanderthals. The main reason for that is a sparse fossil record.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-black-hole.title: Black holes spinning near maximum rate could split in two, calculations suggest
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-black-hole.summary: Two black holes can collide and merge into one. But could the opposite happen: could a single black hole split into two smaller ones? That question is explored in a new theoretical study: "When Black Holes Admit Pair-of-pants Topologies," published in the journal Physical Review D.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-hoarders-b.title: Hoarders without borders: Study suggests investors aid international expansion
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-hoarders-b.summary: Venture capital firms can help young businesses expand internationally by providing funding as well as market knowledge, expertise and access to professional networks, according to a research literature review published in the International Journal of Management and Enterprise Development.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-sea-anemon.title: From sea anemone to human fertility: A new research organism for understanding meiosis
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-sea-anemon.summary: Every egg cell and sperm cell depends on meiosis, a tightly choreographed process in which chromosomes find their partners, exchange genetic material and then divide. When meiosis goes awry in humans, the consequences can include infertility, miscarriage and birth defects.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ancient-vi.title: An ancient virus in chimpanzee DNA switches off a gene that is active in humans
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ancient-vi.summary: Humans and chimpanzees share almost all their genes. Despite this, our brains have developed in different ways. Researchers at Lund University in Sweden have now shown that a viral pandemic dating back several million years is likely to be part of the explanation.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-communitie.title: As flood risk rises, some communities question the idea of resilience
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-communitie.summary: Climate change is increasing flood risk across the U.K. As floods become more frequent and intense, communities are increasingly encouraged to become resilient and "live with water." Yet in some flood-prone areas, residents are rejecting these calls, concerned that resilience is less about helping communities and more about transferring responsibility from institutions to citizens.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-paleolithi.title: Paleolithic human DNA reveals east-west connections across Ice Age Europe
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-paleolithi.summary: More than 30,000 years ago, people associated with one of Europe's major Paleolithic cultures (the Gravettian) were more interconnected than previously thought. An international research team led by the University of Vienna has uncovered new genetic evidence of long-distance connections between these populations. Published in Science Advances, the study combines genomic data from rare human remains with human DNA preserved in cave sediments.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists.title: Scientists find key to predicting some El Niño events 12 months ahead
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists.summary: Scientists have identified the conditions that make it possible to predict some El Niño and La Niña events up to a year in advance, potentially giving communities and decision-makers significantly more time to prepare for weather extremes.

https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ai-math-pr.title: AI is solving math problems that stumped humans. What comes next?
https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ai-math-pr.summary: A few short years ago, asking AI to add two four-digit numbers together for a third-grade math assignment would have been a bad idea. Over half the time, the answer would be wrong, studies have shown. Long division or a "leaky tank" problem, an algebra class staple? Forget about it.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.title: Diagnostic test could help doctors refine prostate cancer treatment
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-d.summary: Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in men—in 2013, it affected more than 1 million men across the world. The cancer does not behave the same way in every patient, and doctors have long faced a difficult balancing act between identifying patients who will benefit from more intensive treatment and those who may do just as well without it. Treating someone more aggressively than necessary is associated with increased side effects and poorer quality of life.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.title: Reprogramming tumor microenvironment could improve prospects for treatment of pancreatic cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-r.summary: Pancreatic cancer is one of the most aggressive and difficult-to-treat cancers. One reason for its resistance to therapy is the dense tissue surrounding the tumor that acts as a protective barrier and suppresses the immune response. It is a complex tissue made of supporting cells, blood vessels and immune cells—the tumor microenvironment. In pancreatic cancer, this surrounding tissue accounts for up to 90% of the tumor mass.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.title: Tegoprubart preserves kidney function better than tacrolimus in first-time transplant patients, trial suggests
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-t.summary: The phase 2 BESTOW clinical trial showed that tegoprubart (a novel anti-CD40L antibody therapy) was better at preserving kidney function than tacrolimus (the current standard of care) in immunosuppressive regimens in adults receiving their first kidney transplant. Kidney graft function stabilized after the first month of treatment and remained higher in tegoprubart-treated patients than in tacrolimus-treated patients at each reported time point, with a statistically significant kidney function benefit at 18 months. A recent analysis of BESTOW data found that tegoprubart also caused greater improvements in patient-reported health-related quality of life compared with tacrolimus in study parti

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-u.title: US–Mexico border counties face high kidney disease–related mortality and low nephrologist availability
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-u.summary: New research indicates that U.S.–Mexico border counties experience disproportionately elevated rates of death from chronic kidney disease (CKD), alongside reduced availability of nephrologists. The findings will be presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.title: Standard kidney function tests underestimate chronic kidney disease in people with cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-s.summary: New research indicates that commonly used measures of kidney function underestimate the prevalence of chronic kidney disease (CKD) in patients with cancer. The findings will be presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: Melanoma vaccine reduces death or cancer recurrence by 42%
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: In a world-first international trial, adding intismeran, a type of personalized therapeutic cancer vaccine made from each patient's own tumor, to pembrolizumab immunotherapy after surgery for high-risk melanoma reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 42%.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.title: 5 great cardio workouts you can do at home
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-g.summary: You might have heard that cardio, or aerobic, exercise is one of the best ways to keep your heart, lungs and cardiovascular system healthy and strong.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-o.title: Online resources and coaching helped people seek genetic testing for cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-o.summary: About 10% of cancers are linked to an inherited genetic variant, but as few as one in 15 cancer patients eligible for genetic testing complete it.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: Study identifies potential new treatment targets for the most common type of bowel cancer
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: Research published today identifies potential new ways to treat the most common type of colorectal cancer in Ireland. The study, conducted by an international research team led by RCSI University of Medicine and Health Sciences and The Institute of Cancer Research, London, provides a roadmap for repurposing existing drugs and developing new ones to create more effective, personalized treatments for thousands of patients who currently have limited options.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.title: A precision T-cell therapy stalls treatment-resistant cancers in clinical trial
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-p.summary: Early results of the first clinical trial to evaluate the drug invikafusp alfa (invika) in humans indicate that the treatment may be capable of managing cancers that have rebuffed most other interventions, including standard immunotherapy.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-y.title: A third of young adults turn to AI for substance-use information
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-y.summary: More than 32% of participants in a Rutgers study reported using ChatGPT and similar chatbots for substance-use information.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.title: Could fish consumption reduce the risk of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy?
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-f.summary: A new prospective study from Japan explored whether fish consumption before and during pregnancy is linked to hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, including gestational hypertension and preeclampsia. Researchers analyzed data from women in Japan, examining fish consumption and n-3 and n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) intake across different stages of pregnancy. The results reveal a pattern that may have implications for preconception and prenatal nutrition.

https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.title: Mental health disparities persist for LGBTQ+ college students nationwide, largest study of its kind finds
https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-10-m.summary: LGBTQ+ college students who experience discrimination are significantly more likely to experience depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts and to avoid needed health care, according to a new national study by Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health, Boston University School of Public Health and Harvard Pilgrim Health Care Institute. https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Could lowering high blood pressure be as simple as stimulating your ear?
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A small device that gently stimulates nerves through the ear could offer a new way to tackle stubborn high blood pressure. https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: A small device that delivers gentle electrical pulses through the ear could offer a new approach to treating stubborn high blood pressure. In a clinical trial led by researchers at Queen Mary University of London, the technology proved safe, well tolerated, and practical for patients to use at home. Although the treatment did not significantly lower blood pressure compared with a placebo device across all participants, researchers observed encouraging results in patients with more severe hypertension. The findings suggest that stimulating nerves in the ear could eventually help certain people whose blood pressure remains elevated despite taking medication. The results come from the SCRATCH-HTN trial, published in Hypertension , a journal of the American Heart Association. Researchers emphasize that larger studies are needed to determine whether the approach can provide meaningful benefits and which patients might respond best. The experimental treatment uses a technique called transcutaneous autonomic neuromodulation (tAN), which aims to influence the autonomic nervous system. This network of nerves automatically controls essential bodily functions, including heart rate, digestion, and blood pressure. By delivering mild electrical signals to nerves in the ear, researchers hope to influence the body's natural mechanisms for regulating blood pressure without requiring an invasive procedure. The handheld device, developed by Afferent Medical Solutions, uses two small clips positioned on the tragus, the small flap of cartilage located just in front of the ear canal. These clips deliver gentle electrical stimulation, allowing patients to administer the treatment themselves without visiting a clinic. The clinical trial, funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), enrolled 63 people with uncontrolled hypertension. All participants were already taking at least one medication to lower their blood pressure, but their readings remained above recommended levels. Researchers randomly divided the participants into two groups. One received active nerve stimulation, while the other used a sham device designed to serve as a comparison. This approach helped investigators assess whether the electrical stimulation produced benefits beyond those associated with using the device itself. Participants used their assigned devices for 30 minutes daily during the first two weeks. For the following 10 weeks, they reduced their sessions to once per week. The results showed that the treatment was safe and generally comfortable for participants. Most also followed the prescribed schedule, suggesting that the technology could be practical for regular use at home. However, when researchers compared blood pressure changes across the entire study population, they found no statistically significant difference between patients receiving active stimulation and those using the sham device. Despite the lack of a significant overall benefit, the researchers identified a potentially important finding among participants who entered the trial with more severe hypertension. A prespecified subgroup analysis, meaning the researchers had planned this comparison before examining the results, revealed a greater reduction in blood pressure among these patients when they received active nerve stimulation rather than the sham treatment. This finding raises the possibility that the technique may work better for people with particularly difficult-to-control blood pressure. However, the trial was relatively small, and the subgroup results require confirmation in larger studies before any conclusions can be drawn about its effectiveness. Dr. Ajay Gupta, Chief Investigator, Clinical Reader at Queen Mary University of London and Consultant Physician at Barts Health NHS Trust, said: "This is an exciting, highly patient-acceptable technology that could ultimately provide a cheap, scalable solution for millions. Although the trial did not achieve significance across the broad unselected group, those with more severe hypertension exhibited a clear blood pressure reduction in the active group compared to sham. "As the first and most thorough study of its kind, this points towards important new research directions that could help us understand whether non-invasive neuromodulation can benefit particular groups of patients with uncontrolled hypertension." High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, is a major contributor to cardiovascular disease and increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes. It places additional strain on blood vessels and the heart, potentially causing serious damage over time. Although medications help many patients manage their condition, a substantial number continue to have blood pressure readings above recommended targets even while receiving treatment. This ongoing challenge has encouraged scientists to explore additional approaches that could complement existing therapies. Ear nerve stimulation is one such possibility. Because the device is small, does not require surgery, and can be used at home, it could offer a convenient option if future research establishes that it reliably lowers blood pressure in certain patients. For now, the findings represent an early step rather than proof of an effective new treatment. The researchers say larger clinical trials will be essential to confirm the encouraging results in patients with severe hypertension and identify which groups, if any, could benefit most from this approach. https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: This 150-million-year-old bird had dinosaur teeth and a strange secret
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A 150-million-year-old fossil discovered in China reveals a bizarre early bird with sharp teeth, a dinosaur-like claw, and a body built for life on the ground rather than flight. https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.text: A remarkably preserved 150-million-year-old bird fossil discovered in China is challenging long-standing ideas about how birds evolved. Rather than developing increasingly sophisticated flight abilities, some of the earliest birds appear to have taken a very different evolutionary path, including losing the ability to fly altogether. The newly identified species, Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis , lived during the Late Jurassic period (150-148 million years ago). Described in a study published in Nature, the crow-sized creature provides evidence that early bird evolution was much more complex than scientists once believed. Instead of evolving primarily to become better flyers, ancient birds were adapting to a variety of environments and ways of life, including those that favored living on the ground. Researchers from the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology (IVPP) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) and the Fujian Institute of Geological Sciences uncovered the fossil in the recently recognized Zhenghe Fauna of Fujian Province in southeastern China. According to their findings, Yuezhuornis represents the earliest known example of a bird lineage losing its ability to fly. One of the most remarkable features of Yuezhuornis is its unusual combination of bird and dinosaur characteristics. Although it possessed skeletal features associated with birds, it also retained anatomical traits that would have been familiar among small predatory dinosaurs. Its jaws contained closely spaced, serrated teeth resembling those of deinonychosaurs, a group of meat-eating dinosaurs that included agile predators related to birds. Such teeth are not normally associated with early birds. Even more striking was its second toe, which could bend backward unusually far and carried a curved, sickle-shaped claw. This specialized feature is strongly associated with deinonychosaurs, including dromaeosaurids and troodontids, two groups of predatory dinosaurs. "When we examined Yuezhuornis , we were struck by its extraordinary mix of features," said Dr. Min Wang, corresponding author of the study. "It possesses bird-like pelvic and hindlimb structures yet retains the specialized predatory foot and teeth of a small meat-eating dinosaur. It shows us that early bird evolution was far more complicated than we previously realized." To understand how Yuezhuornis was related to other prehistoric birds and dinosaurs, scientists carried out detailed analyses of its evolutionary relationships. They used two approaches, maximum parsimony and Bayesian tip-dating, to compare anatomical characteristics and reconstruct the species' position on the evolutionary tree. Maximum parsimony identifies evolutionary relationships that require the fewest changes in characteristics, while Bayesian tip-dating also incorporates statistical estimates of evolutionary history and information about when fossils lived. Both methods produced consistent results, placing Yuezhuornis within Avialae, the evolutionary group that includes modern birds and their closest extinct relatives. "The results consistently placed Yuezhuornis firmly within Avialae (the group containing modern birds and their closest extinct relatives), just crownward of Archaeopteryx and as a sister taxon to Zhengheornis," said Dr. Zhonghe Zhou, a co-author of the study. This placement is particularly important because Archaeopteryx, which also lived roughly 150 million years ago, is among the most famous early bird relatives. The findings indicate that Yuezhuornis belonged to an early branch of bird evolution rather than simply being a small predatory dinosaur with bird-like characteristics. The researchers also examined how Yuezhuornis might have lived. Using measurements of its skeletal proportions and statistical comparisons with other animals, they investigated whether its anatomy was better suited for flying or moving along the ground. The results showed that its limb proportions closely resembled those of modern ground-dwelling birds and certain other prehistoric dinosaurs closely related to birds. This similarity suggests that Yuezhuornis spent its life on the ground and was likely unable to fly. The findings point to an unexpected development in the history of birds. Rather than simply progressing toward stronger wings and more efficient flight, some early bird lineages appear to have moved in the opposite direction, adapting to lifestyles in which flying was no longer necessary. This challenges the traditional assumption that the earliest stages of bird evolution were driven primarily by the demands of flight. Instead, birds were already exploring different ecological roles and developing a surprisingly wide range of body forms. The discovery of Yuezhuornis suggests that the evolution of birds was never a simple, one-directional process. Even during the Late Jurassic, when the earliest bird lineages were emerging, some species were developing adaptations that favored life on land rather than in the air. Its unusual combination of bird-like anatomy, dinosaur-style predatory features, and apparent flightlessness provides a revealing glimpse into that evolutionary experimentation. The fossil shows that early birds were more anatomically and ecologically diverse than previously recognized. It also underscores the scientific importance of the Zhenghe Fauna, a fossil assemblage that is helping researchers investigate a poorly understood period in bird evolution. As additional discoveries emerge from this region of China, scientists may gain an even clearer picture of the surprising evolutionary paths taken by the earliest birds. https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.title: Low-dose aspirin linked to 70% lower dementia risk, but there's a catch
https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/1.summary: A common, inexpensive medication could hold an unexpected clue to preventing dementia. Researchers found that older adults with a specific genetic profile had a 70% lower relative risk of dementia when taking low-dose aspirin, even though previous studies found no overall protective effect.
